content.summary_of_the_paper: The aim of this paper is to propose a new framework based on latent factor analysis for modeling functional MRI data from the human somatomotor cortex. The proposed model can use whole-brain data to discover the unstudied dynamical latent factors. The primary claim here is extending temporal ICA to the non-linear deep learning model that generalizes weight sharing to non-Euclidean neuroimaging data. Overall, I found this paper difficult to follow, and I am not sure from the standpoint of machine learning how the proposed method is a novel one.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: Please refer to the review section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Please refer to the review section.
content.summary_of_the_review:
a) The paper might have some practical applications, but it is unclear whether its contribution(s) will be recognized as part of the machine learning field. 

b) The performance of the proposed method should be compared with similar state-of-the-art approaches, e.g., SRM (Chen 2015), DHA (Yousefnezhad 2017), HTFA (Manning 2018), ShICA (Richard 2021), etc.

c) There are some correlation results (Fig. 2) and some visualizations (Figs. 3 and 4) reported in empirical studies without supporting numerical results to back them up. Please provide us with some robust machine learning evaluation of your model, for example, a cross-validated classification analysis. 

d) What is the axis X in Figure 2? What are the upper and lower bounds?

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose a nonlinear temporal ICA considering weight sharing utilizing hemispheric symmetry, geodesics as distance measure, and inductive priors on functional activation analyzing fMRI data pertaining to somatomotor cortex in humans. In particular, the proposed approach utilizes a VAE with spatial weight-sharing akin to CNN but using the surface morphology along the geodesics for the kernels. To impose temporal independence an additional KL-term is introduced assuming temporal independence and the deviation from independence imposed using a regularization factor \beta. The approach is contrasted conventional temporal ICA and \beta-VAE on data from the Human Connectome Project in recovering spatial activations and dynamic task signatures.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:
The approach is sound and clearly the use of geodesics, weight sharing and temporal independence are useful inductive biases as also highlighted by the results.
A procedure is given to provide spatial maps from the latent representations using variance of the spatial maps by systematically increasing each latent factor providing sound spatial representations.
The approach can integrate hemispheric geometric properties explicitly through weight sharing. 

Weaknesses:
Whereas tICA is a very simple and explainable model it is generally more challenging to interpret representations learned in the proposed TI-VAE. This should be discussed. Although the performance is better than tICA it is only marginally so and for low values of \beta substantially worse. It is therefore unclear how much is gained presently from the proposed procedure when compared to the much simpler tICA approach.

There is a vast body of work on the use of deep learning autoencoders for fMRI data. The paper does not cover all of this literature and includes very limited experimental comparisons presently to tICA and \beta-VAE. 
(Existing work on task-based auto-encoding of fMRI includes:
Huang, Heng, et al. "Modeling task fMRI data via deep convolutional autoencoder." IEEE transactions on medical imaging 37.7 (2017): 1551-1561.)
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Code are planned to be publicly released and data used openly available from the Human Connectome Project promoting reproducibility. The paper is clearly written but the novelty somewhat limited.

Minor comments:
Abstract: Then, to evaluate the latent factors we find further, we compare… ->
Then, in order to evaluate the latent factors, we compare…

Figure 2A: Please include \beta on the x-axis.
It is also unclear exactly what beta-VAE refers to please elaborate exactly how this procedure is specified – using Euclidean as opposed to geodesic geometry? Less weight sharing?
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper appears somewhat incremental combining geodesic geometry, weight sharing and temporal independence for improved non-linear inference of latent dynamics in fMRI. The experimental evaluation is based on recovery of bold signal as specified by the canonical HRF and spatial maps corresponding to regions activated but the evaluation limited to comparisons to tICA and beta-VAE.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes a methodology for disentangled unsupervised latent factor analysis of somatosensory fMRI during motor tasks as a non-linear alternative to independent component analysis. A recurrent encoder and a variation decoder are used, with a sort of weight sharing across voxels within the same clusters. ELBO with an additional total correlation penalty for the latent dimensions is used for training. Two types of clusters based on structural and functional connectivity are compared. Results show that the spatial map, identified by the sensitivity of the decoder to the latent dimensions, are anatomically meaningful. The correlation (of possibly the group average) of the best matched latent factor with the ground truth was higher than those from ICA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
The idea of dynamic latent factor analysis for fMRI is interesting and the use of a VAE that produces more independent factors is meaningful. 
The approach for analyzing the cortical surface data is interesting.
The method for visualizing the spatial maps is interesting. 
The results confirm that this independence is important. 

Weaknesses:
The paper is verbally dense. Key parts of the methodology are not discussed in the body. 
The paper leaves with many questions that I have as a reader (and as a reviewer).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Novelty:
The paper has novelty in applying the ideas of VAEs with disentangled to fMRI tasks with real data. This along with the graph based clustering approaches on both structural and functional connectivity to promote weight sharing could be novel. 

Reproducibility:
The paper states code release, but reproducibility could be limited by issues with clarity and unclear methods for the experimental design (train / test split),  selection hyper-parameters, etc.

Quality: 
The papers performs experiments on a single dataset with a rather complicated model. The results are empirical and the contribution is a specific framework. Some baselines are explored. The quality could be improved by better clarity of the methodology including hyper-parameter selection and ablations. 

Clarity: 
The paper has many minor issues with clarity. 

The introduction reasoning is quite dense. Initially it is not clear what geodesics are involved. 

HCP in introduction is not defined. 

The word sense of 'null models' is not clear to me. Is this referring to the null hypothesis? 

What is the depth of the cortical surface in terms of voxels? 

How is the data randomly shuffled? There are many divisions of the data set in time that would break the temporal dependence.  Is this across subjects? 

What is 'average temporal time series for the unseen test set' mean? Does this mean that the test set is only tested on a group level not individual?  Likewise the definition of 'absolute average correlation' is not clear.  Mathematical formulation would be preferred. 

Before (1), missing 'covariance' in  "unit-norm diagonal multivariate Gaussian" 

The choice of generative model has to be a Gaussian for the likelihood to be inversely proportional to the mean squared error.  The assumption of Gaussianity (or equivalent) should be stated. 

The verbal description on the top of page 4 could be aided by mathematical notation. 

In the "importance of weight sharing" subsection, the analogies are hard to follow for a reader not a familiar with the sizes of large models trained on ImageNet. Overall, this analogy seems tangential. Furthermore, hidden in this paragraph are a description of using "MLPs  to each cluster". Clustering hasn't been mentioned yet.

The phrasing  " Each patch is shared among the 9 weights of the kernel" seems to be backwards. The weights are shared by the patches... 

Spectral clustering is not mentioned in the body. No citation or description of the methodology is given. How many clusters are used, etc.? 

The pictorial representation in Figure 1 is not clear, especially on the right. It doesn't seem to indicate the hidden sizes for each layer as given in the text. 	

It should be stated that the hyper-parameters beyond the epoch are also selected using validation. 

In Figure 2(A)  Beta-VAE adapted to the time series case with the same weight sharing? Is the only difference the total correlation in the objective?

What is the number of factors in Figure 2(B)? 

From Figure 2(B) it looks like ICA's factors are not completely disentangled. A stronger baseline may be to see the correlation of a linear fit to the ground truth. That is ICA may be capturing the factors but they are not as disentangled as the proposed approach. 

At the start of the Section 3, it is suggested that the weight sharing is discussed, but it is no clear what the comparison is besides the two (functional and structural) versus each other. 

In "Task dynamics" "subsequently"->"sequentially" ? 

 With tSNE results, perplexity and the number of points plotted should be stated.  Note that relative arrangement of modes in tSNE is not reliable and interpretation of them may not be stable. 

In conclusion, "whole brain" is mentioned, but this is only the cortical surface. 

References have some issues in formatting. Use parenthetical citations when author names not being used as part of sentence. 

Typeset variables consistently (if it is italics then it should be italics inline too). 

In the "weight sharing" subsection use $\times$ instead of $x$.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper adopts a VAE approach with total correlation penalty that yields meaningful latent factors on task fMRI data. Additional adjustments for weight sharing using clustering of the cortical surface voxels is used but the details are not clear. The paper is verbally dense, which gives the reader much context, but also many questions on the specifics. It seems like a thorough revision to clarify is necessary.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a framework that uses the sequential variational autoencoder to analyze the dynamics of the task fMRI data the HCP dataset. The framework aims to perform latent factor analysis in a way similar to traditional ICA but in a deep learning scheme. A 'weight-sharing' strategy was proposed to make the learning more effective. The learned spatial maps are compared with those derived from traditional ICA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength

* Linear ICA was extended to a non-liner version based on auto-encoder learning framework. 

* $\beta$-VAE was used disentangle latent factors

# Weakness

* Using VAE-like networks to extend ICA analysis of fMRI to a non-linear fashion is not novel. A wide variety of prior studies have been done on this. E.g., Huang et al.  "Modeling Task fMRI Data Via Deep Convolutional Autoencoder" and Kim et al. "Representation learning of resting state fmri with variational autoencoder". None of the SOTA fMRI methods were included other than $\beta$-VAE.

* The validation does not really indicate the effectiveness of the proposed approach. If traditional ICA was the pseudo ground truth, why would we need a new approach? Experiments were qualitative so it becomes hard to know whether the results are accurate or not.

* The novelty seems to lie in the way vertices are grouped together by graph clustering. There were already extensively efforts in defining hierarchical parcellation of the cortex based on the HCP data (e.g., MMP atlas) using structural and functional affinity across vertices. There were no experiments justifying the need and advantage of the new clustering scheme.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: I would rate the clarity and reproducibility low. The key proposal 'weight sharing' was only vaguely described. In the end I was having a hard time understanding what weights were shared across what components as there was no algorithmic nor mathematical definition of the weight sharing strategy. Cortex parcellation on graphs (surfaces) considering both structural and functional affinity was a widely explored topic so I do not see too much novelty herein.
content.summary_of_the_review: The writing of the manuscript needs to be improved in stringently describing the weight sharing operation and how it was integrated with the rest of the network. Given that the limited experimental results were all qualitative and not convincing, I would consider this work preliminary.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
